defaults.permitted_development: For a house in Wales, a modest porch is usually permitted development if it stays within the 3 square metre, 3m high and highway-boundary limits and no local restriction has removed the right.

rules.height_rules: The key height limit is 3m overall, measured in the same way as a house extension. There is no extra allowance for a pitched or feature porch roof once it passes that height.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance. The main size test is external ground floor area, which should not exceed 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: No part of the porch should be within 2m of a boundary with a highway. Always check whether a planning condition or Article 4 direction has removed the right for the property.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance beyond the overall footprint and 3m height limit. Any porch roof design must sit within those national limits.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that sit naturally with the host house. Listed building consent may still be required where heritage significance would be affected.

rules.permitted_development: Welsh permitted development can normally cover a porch when it remains very small: up to 3 square metres externally, up to 3m high and not within 2m of the boundary with the highway.

rules.height_rules: Whatever roof form is chosen, the porch should stay within a 3m overall height cap measured in the same way as a house extension.
rules.depth_rules: Porches do not get a dedicated projection allowance in Wales. The practical size test is that the external ground-floor footprint must stay at or below 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: Check the relationship to the highway boundary first. On many front elevations, the porch dimensions may be fine but the required 2m separation to the highway boundary is what determines the answer.
rules.roof_rules: A porch roof does not get its own Welsh allowance. The overall porch, including any projecting canopy, still has to fit within the 3 square metre and 3m limits.
rules.materials_rules: Because porches are usually prominent from the street, external materials and detailing should sit comfortably with the house. A restrained palette is often safest in sensitive settings.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Wales, conservation area controls and any Article 4 direction can remove normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check the planning register before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: A small porch can often use the normal Welsh householder right where the footprint is no more than 3 square metres, the overall height is no more than 3m and the structure stays at least 2m from the highway boundary.

rules.height_rules: Porch height is capped at 3m overall in Wales. A pitched roof, canopy or decorative form does not create a separate allowance beyond that maximum.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not assessed by a standalone projection figure. The controlling size limit is the overall external ground-floor area of 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: The 2m highway-boundary rule is often the critical Welsh test on tight plots. If the house already sits close to the street or pavement, even a small porch can fall outside the ordinary right.
rules.roof_rules: Roof design is secondary to the small-porch limits: the whole structure must still stay within 3 square metres externally and 3m in height. Canopy-heavy designs can fail even where the enclosed space looks modest.
rules.materials_rules: The best porch designs usually look like a natural extension of the entrance rather than a bolt-on box. Matching or carefully complementary materials often matter most on the front elevation.

rules.boundary_rules: Check the relationship to the highway boundary first. On many front elevations, the porch dimensions may be fine but the required 2m separation to the highway boundary is what determines the answer.
rules.roof_rules: A porch roof does not get its own Welsh allowance. The overall porch, including any projecting canopy, still has to fit within the 3 square metre and 3m limits.
rules.materials_rules: Because porches are usually prominent from the street, external materials and detailing should sit comfortably with the house. A restrained palette is often safest in sensitive settings.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Wales, conservation area controls and any Article 4 direction can remove normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check the planning register before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: For a house in Wales, a modest porch is usually permitted development if it stays within the 3 square metre, 3m high and highway-boundary limits and no local restriction has removed the right.

rules.height_rules: The key height limit is 3m overall, measured in the same way as a house extension. There is no extra allowance for a pitched or feature porch roof once it passes that height.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance. The main size test is external ground floor area, which should not exceed 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: No part of the porch should be within 2m of a boundary with a highway. Always check whether a planning condition or Article 4 direction has removed the right for the property.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance beyond the overall footprint and 3m height limit. Any porch roof design must sit within those national limits.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that sit naturally with the host house. Listed building consent may still be required where heritage significance would be affected.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, conservation area and wider protected landscape controls mean visible external changes should be checked with the authority before relying on permitted development.
restrictions.listed_building: If the property or a curtilage structure is listed in Bannau Brycheiniog, listed building consent may be needed even for relatively modest works affecting character.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: A small porch can often use the normal Welsh householder right where the footprint is no more than 3 square metres, the overall height is no more than 3m and the structure stays at least 2m from the highway boundary.

rules.height_rules: Porch height is capped at 3m overall in Wales. A pitched roof, canopy or decorative form does not create a separate allowance beyond that maximum.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not assessed by a standalone projection figure. The controlling size limit is the overall external ground-floor area of 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: The 2m highway-boundary rule is often the critical Welsh test on tight plots. If the house already sits close to the street or pavement, even a small porch can fall outside the ordinary right.
rules.roof_rules: Roof design is secondary to the small-porch limits: the whole structure must still stay within 3 square metres externally and 3m in height. Canopy-heavy designs can fail even where the enclosed space looks modest.
rules.materials_rules: The best porch designs usually look like a natural extension of the entrance rather than a bolt-on box. Matching or carefully complementary materials often matter most on the front elevation.
